title: Work and Energy
text:
Objectives
Work describes a transfer of energy between systems. Work can change the kinetic energy of a system or its potential energy. Although work can transfer energy between systems, Newton’s laws imply that the total energy in the universe is conserved. This yields the work-energy theorem: \(W = \Delta K + \Delta U.\)
This lab consists of two parts.
Keep detailed notes. Record your setup, procedure, data, and observations in your lab notebook. Data will include tables and plots. In your memo, summarize your findings and discuss any conclusions you draw from your data.

title: Work and Energy
text:
Impulse, Work, and Energy
Some of the motion carts in the lab are equipped with a launcher. The launcher provides a reasonably reproducible force each time it is used.
Discuss the following questions with your group before you begin taking measurements.

How can you measure the impulse \(\vec{J}\) generated by the launcher?
How can you measure the work \(W\) done by the launcher?
Do you think the launcher delivers the same impulse each time it is used?
Do you think the launcher does the same amount of work each time it is used?
If you double the mass of a cart, what will happen to the final speed of the cart?
What would a plot of final velocity versus mass look like?

Use a motion cart to measure the impulse and work for at least five different cart masses. Take multiple measurements for each mass and make your best estimate of the impulse and work generated by the launcher.
Make a plot of final velocity versus mass of the cart.

Did the launcher deliver the same impulse each time it was used?
Did the launcher do the same work each time it was used?

title: Work and Energy

Conservation of Energy
The principle of conservation of energy is this: The total energy in a closed system is constant.
Work with your lab group to design an experiment to investigate the conservation of energy. Your experiment should include the following elements.

A system in which both potential and kinetic energy can change
A theoretical prediction that you can test with measurements
A numerical test of conservation of energy

Keep a good record of your work. Someone reading your notebook should be able to replicate your work and verify your findings.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Objectives
In this lab, we will explore two-dimensional kinematics, the mathematical analysis of motion in two dimensions. Our focus will be the motion of a projectile. You will investigate a launcher, and then make a mathematical model to predict where a projectile will land when the launcher is inclined to a specific launch angle. When you are satisfied with your model, you will use it to hit a target selected by your instructor.
There are three stages of this investigation:
You can — and should — apply your knowledge of kinematics in this lab.
Record your setup, procedure, data, and observations in your lab notes. Keep detailed notes. Data for this lab will include data tables and plots. In your memo, summarize your findings and describe how you tackled the design and measurement problems of this lab.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Safety
The launching device is a spring gun. It is part of an apparatus called a ballistic pendulum. We will not be using the pendulum this week — only the launcher. The spring gun will fire a solid metal sphere at a moderate speed, so some precautions are in order.

Always make certain you have a clear path before launching a projectile.
Never load the spring gun until you are ready to fire.
Never walk in front of a loaded spring gun.

In other words, use common sense. Be certain no human is in the line of fire.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Investigate the Launcher
Your objective is to hit a target by adjusting the position and launch angle of the spring gun. As a first step toward this goal, you should investigate the following:

the range of a horizontal shot
the spread in impact points for “identical” initial conditions

To conclude this portion of the lab, use your knowledge of kinematics and the range of a horizontal shot to calculate the initial speed of the projectile as it leaves the launcher. Remember: When a projectile is fired horizontally, it moves with constant velocity in the horizontal direction and falls with constant acceleration in the vertical direction.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Investigate Range and Inclination
In this portion of the lab, you will gather data and model the range of the projectile as a function of launch angle. Before you begin taking measurements, adjust the location of your spring gun for maximum range. You should be able to hit points as close as \(1\,\mathsf{m}\) and as far as the barricade.
You will have to determine how to investigate a range of inclinations and how to interpret your data. (Part of experimental science and engineering is imagining what you could do if you had the ideal equipment. The more important part is accomplishing your objective with the materials available!)
Use your data to predict where the projectile will land for a given launch angle. Once you are confident in your model, practice hitting targets of your own. When you are satisfied, you may move on to the final stage.

title: Projectile Motion
text:

Your instructor will place a small target a fixed distance from the launcher. Your group will then adjust your launcher to hit the target.

title: Fluid Simulations
text:
Objectives
Fluid mechanics is a vast and complex subject, but it is built upon the laws of physics we have learned this term. For example, the buoyant force on an object can be derived by applying Newton’s Second Law, and Bernoulli’s Principle is equivalent to the conservation of energy. In this lab, we will investigate some of these properties.
The lab consists of three parts.
You will investigate three different simulations today. Keep detailed notes. Record your procedure, data, and observations in your lab notes. Data will include tables and plots. In your memo, summarize your findings and discuss any conclusions you draw from your data.

title: Fluid Simulations
text:
Buoyant Force
The density of an object is its mass divided by its volume: \(\rho = M/V\). Objects that are less dense than water will float, and those that are more dense will sink. But what is the nature of the buoyant force?
Open the Force Buoyancy Lab simulation from The Physics Aviary. This simulation allows you to measure the force on an object as it is lowered into a fluid. Play with this simulation to see how it works. The force required to suspend the bottle is plotted below the animation.
Observe. What happens to the force as you lower the bottle into the water?
Measure. You can vary the mass and volume of the bottle, to adjust its density. Set the volume of the bottle to its maximum value of \(600\,\mathsf{mL}\) and set the fluid to “Fresh Water”, and then carry out the following measurements.

Construct three bottles with a density greater than \(1.0\,\mathsf{g/cm^3}\), and record the weight of the bottle and the minimum force.
Construct three bottles with a density less than \(1.0\,\mathsf{g/cm^3}\), and record the weight of the bottle and the minimum force.

Note that \(1\,\mathsf{mL} = 1\,\mathsf{cm^3}\).
Analyze. The buoyant force on the object is the difference between its dry weight (the maximum force reading) and its submerged weight (the minimum force reading). Compute the buoyant force you measured for all six objects. Summarize your findings and describe any patterns you notice in your memo.
For theoretical background on this simulation, see Section 14.4 of OpenStax — Volume 1.

title: Fluid Simulations
text:
Fluid Columns
When applying Newton’s laws to solid objects, we focus on the force on an object and the mass of an object. When dealing with fluids, we focus on the pressure in the fluid and the density of a fluid instead. The concepts are related: pressure is force per unit area (\(P = F/A\)) and density is mass per unit volume (\(\rho = M/V\)). But the differences lead to some interesting effects with fluids.
Open the Fluids in U-Tube Lab from The Physics Aviary. In this simulation, we will examine two columns of fluid connected by a tube. It is similar to a balance or seesaw, but has fluid on either side instead of solid objects.
Predict. Before you begin, consider the following questions.

If you have columns of the same fluid on either side and each column has the same radius, will the final heights of the two columns be the same?
If you have columns of the same fluid on either side and each column has a different radius, will the final heights of the two columns be the same?
If you have columns of different fluids on either side and each column has the same radius, will the final heights of the two columns be the same?
If you have columns of the different fluids on either side and each column has a different radius, will the final heights of the two columns be the same?
Can you set up the experiment so that the final height of columns of different fluids will be the same?

Test. Do a series of experiments to test your hypotheses. Keep notes of your setup for each trial and your results. Remember that a single test does not confirm a hypothesis, though it may disprove it.
Analyze. Based on your measurements — including any additional measurements you choose to make — what factors determine the final heights of the columns of fluid in this experiment?
Be sure to discuss any differences between your predictions and your observations in your memo.
For theoretical background on this simulation, see Section 14.3 of OpenStax — Volume 1.

Fluid Flow
In this last set of experiments, we will examine properties of a flowing fluid. Open the Fluid Dynamics Lab from The Physics Aviary. This simulation allows us to examine how the diameter and pressure in a pipe affect the speed of a flowing fluid.
Predict. Think about and answer the following questions before you begin taking measurements.

What will happen to the speed of the fluid on the right as you increase the pressure on the left?
What will happen to the pressure in the fluid on the right as you increase the pressure on the left?
What will happen to the speed and pressure on the right as you decrease the radius of the pipe on the left?
How can you make the pressure on the right as large as possible?
How can you make the speed on the right as large as possible?

Test. Do a series of experiments to test your hypotheses. Keep notes of your setup for each trial and your results. Remember that a single test does not confirm a hypothesis, though it may disprove it.
Analyze. Based on your measurements — including any additional measurements you choose to make — what factors determine the speed of the fluid in this experiment?
Be sure to discuss any differences between your predictions and your observations in your memo.
For theoretical background on this simulation, see Sections 14.5–6 of OpenStax — Volume 1.

title: Simple Machines Simulations
text:
Objectives
Simple machines are devices that change the direction or magnitude of an applied force. Renaissance scholars identified six such machines. We will explore three today: the pulley, the ramp, and the lever.1 Unlike early Renaissance scholars, we have classical mechanics to aid us! We will attempt to analyze these devices using forces, work, and energy.
This lab consists of three major parts
You will investigate three different simulations today. Keep detailed notes. Record your setup, procedure, data, and observations in your lab notes. Data will include tables and plots. In your memo, summarize your findings and discuss any conclusions you draw from your data.

title: Simple Machines Simulations
text:
Mechanical Advantage
A simple machine is a device for redirecting or multiplying a force. We often think of such machines in terms of the applied force and the load. The applied force is the force you put into the machine. The load is the force the machine applies to something else. In this lab, it will be the weight you lift.
The mechanical advantage of a machine is the ratio of the load to the applied force:
                           load
mechanical advantage = -------------
                       applied force
For example, if you apply a force of \(\Quantity{100}{lbs}\) and you are able to lift a load of \(\Quantity{200}{lbs}\), the system has a mechanical advantage of 2: It doubles your applied force. In principle, the mechanical advantage is a constant for a particular machine. Thus, if we measure and plot the load as a function of applied force, the mechanical advantage will be the slope of this line.
Note, however, that conservation of energy implies that the work done by each force be equal in magnitude. When a system is in equilibrium, the net work for any small displacement of the system must be zero. This is known as the principle of virtual work.

title: Simple Machines Simulations
text:
Pulleys
In a simple pulley system, a mass hangs on one side of the pulley (the load) and you apply a force by pulling on a string on the other side of the pulley (the applied force). We can also combine multiple pulleys. The mechanical advantage of the pulley system is the ratio of the load to the applied force.
Open the Pulley Lab from Physics Aviary. Play with this simulation to see how it works. When you are comfortable with the controls, carry out the following investigations.
Predict. Consider the following questions before you make any measurements.

How do you think the mechanical advantage will change with the number of pulleys — if at all? I.e., for a given load, how will the applied force you need to lift that load depend on the number of pulleys?

Measure.

For a fixed mass, measure the applied force for all six pulley combinations. The load is the weight of the hanging mass (\(W=mg\)), and the applied force is the reading on the force sensor. What is the mechanical advantage of each pulley system?

Reflect. Were your predictions correct? Can you explain your findings? In your memo, discuss useful applications for a simple pulley, in light of your measurements.

title: Angular Momentum Simulations
text:
Rolling Motion
In this portion of the experiment, we will investigate how the acceleration of a rolling object depends on its mass, radius, and mass distribution.
Open the Disk Rolling Down Incline simulation from The Physics Aviary. Play with the simulation to see how it works.
We will measure the acceleration using either the velocity graphs or the data points generated by the simulation. Be sure you understand how to measure the acceleration before you proceed to the next step.
When you are ready, proceed to the studies below.
Measure. The goal is to determine which factors have the strongest effect on the acceleration of the object. There are 3 to investigate: Outer Radius, Inner Radius, and Mass. This set of measurements will isolate one variable at a time.

Outer Radius. First, we will investigate the acceleration of solid disks of different sizes. Set the Inner Radius to \(0\,\mathsf{mm}\), and set the mass to a value of your choice. Leave these parameters fixed. Measure the acceleration for three different values of Outer Radius: \(75\,\mathsf{mm}\), \(120\,\mathsf{mm}\), and one intermediate value of your choice.
Inner Radius. Next, we will investigate the acceleration of hollow disks of different shapes. Set the Outer Radius to \(100\,\mathsf{mm}\), and set the mass to a value of your choice. Leave these parameters fixed. Measure the acceleration for three different values of Inner Radius: \(50\,\mathsf{mm}\), \(95\,\mathsf{mm}\), and one other value of your choice.
Mass. Finally, we will investigate the acceleration of hollow disks of different masses. Set the Outer Radius to \(100\,\mathsf{mm}\), and set the Inner Radius to some value of your choice. Leave these parameters fixed. Measure the acceleration for three different values of Mass: \(25\,\mathsf{g}\), \(200\,\mathsf{g}\), and one intermediate value of your choice.

Make more measurements if you are interested. Try to observe how the acceleration depends on the size, shape, and mass of the disk.

Moment of Inertia
The moment of inertia of an object describes its distribution of mass. It affects how easy or difficult it is to make an object rotate, and it is part of the angular momentum of the object. For a point particle of mass \(m\) distance \(r\) from the axis of rotation, the moment of inertia is \(I = mr^2\). The first simulation today will allow you to explore the effect of changing the mass and location of a particle on the rotation of system.
Open the Person on a Rotating Platform simulation from oPhysics. This simulation holds the total angular momentum of the system constant as you adjust the size, mass, and location of the objects in it. Play with the simulation to see how it works, and then carry out the following studies.
Measure.
First, make the “Radius of Cylinder” as large as possible and the “Mass of Cylinder” as small as possible.

Set the mass of the person to \(100\,\mathsf{kg}\) and measure the angular velocity at 5 different settings of “Radius of Person’s Path”: \(0.5\,\mathsf{m}\), \(5.0\,\mathsf{m}\), and 3 intermediate values of your choice.
Set the radius of the person’s path to \(1\,\mathsf{m}\) and measure the angular velocity at 5 different settings of “Mass of Person”: \(50\,\mathsf{kg}\), \(200\,\mathsf{kg}\), and 3 intermediate values of your choice.

Analyze.

Plot your data for Angular Velocity vs. Radius.
Plot your data for Angular Velocity vs. Mass.
What relationships do you observe? Try to be as precise as possible — is it a linear relationship? exponential? power law? Use linear, semilog, and log-log plots to back up your conclusion.

title: Friction Simulations
text:
Objectives
Friction is a ubiquitous phenomenon in the real world, but it is frequently ignored in introductory physics courses. Today, we will examine some of the effects of friction.
This lab consists of three major parts
You will investigate three different simulations today. Keep detailed notes. Record your setup, procedure, data, and observations in your lab notes. Data will include tables and plots. In your memo, summarize your findings and discuss any conclusions you draw from your data.

title: Friction Simulations
text:
Static and Kinetic Friction
Despite the complex interactions that give rise to friction, the force obeys a simple law: \[f = \mu N.\] The force due to friction is directly proportional to the normal force acting on an object. The constant of proportionality, \(\mu\), is called the coefficient of friction. If an object is stationary, the constant is called the coefficient of static friction, and the formula gives the maximum force that can be applied before the object starts slipping. If the object is sliding along, it is called the coefficient of kinetic friction. Typically, the coefficient of kinetic friction is less than the coefficient of static friction: it is harder to get something moving than it is to keep it going.
Open the Friction Lab from Physics Aviary. This simulation provides a force sensor to investigate friction for different blocks and surfaces. The simulation will gradually increase the force you are pulling with until the block starts to slide, then pull the block with constant velocity. Play with the simulation to see how it works.
Predict. Before you start making measurements, consider the following questions.

How can you use the graph of Force vs. Time to determine the coefficients of friction?
What will happen to the force required to move the block if you increase its mass?
What will happen to coefficients of friction if you increase the mass of the block?

Measure.

Determine the coefficients of static friction and kinetic friction for 3 different interfaces.
Investigate the dependence of the forces and coefficients on the mass of the block and orientation of the block. Pick one pair of surfaces and measure the coefficients for 3 different masses: \(100\,\mathsf{g}\), \(2000\,\mathsf{g}\), and one intermediate value of your choice.

Analyze. Summarize your results and discuss your findings in your lab memo.

title: Friction Simulations
text:
Critical Angle
Direct measurements with a spring scale or force sensor provide one way to measure the coefficient of friction. A simple alternative is the following.

Place an object on a board.
Tilt the board until the object starts to slide down.
Use Newton’s Second Law and trig to calculate the coefficient of friction.

The maximum angle \(\theta\) to which you can tilt the ramp before the object starts sliding down is called the critical angle.
We can investigate this relationship with the Forces on an Incline simulation from Physics Aviary. Play with the simulation to see how it works.
Predict. Discuss the following questions before you begin.

What effect will increasing the coefficient of friction have on the critical angle?
What effect will increasing the mass of the block have on the critical angle?

Measure.

Hold the mass constant and measure the critical angle for at least 5 different coefficients of friction.
Hold coefficients of friction constant and measure the critical angle for at least 3 different masses.

Analyze. Summarize your results and discuss your findings in your lab memo.

There is a relation between the critical angle and the coefficient of friction. Make 4 plots and try to determine this relationship:

\(\theta\) vs. \(\mu\)
\(\cos \theta\) vs. \(\mu\)
\(\sin \theta\) vs. \(\mu\)
\(\tan \theta\) vs. \(\mu\)

What trends do you notice in the relationship between critical angle and mass?

title: Friction Simulations
text:
Drag Forces
In the last portion of today’s lab, we will investigate the drag forces in fluids.
Open up the Ball in Viscous Fluid simulation from Andrew Duffy. This simulation gives you control over the properties of a ball bearing and the fluid it is dropped in, and allows you to view its position, velocity, and acceleration graphs. Play around with the simulation to see how it works.
Predict. Before you make any measurements, consider the following questions.

If you drop a ball bearing in air, what will its position, velocity, and acceleration graphs look like?
If you drop the same ball bearing in honey, what will its position, velocity, and acceleration graphs look like as a function of time?
The simulation gives us control over the ball bearing’s density and radius. We can also vary the viscosity by choosing different fluids. (Loosely speaking, the viscosity is the “thickness” of the fluid. It is large for honey, intermediate for oil, and small for water.) title: Collision Simulations
text:
Analyze 2D Collisions
Conservation of Momentum — In any collision, Newton’s Second and Third Laws imply that momentum should be conserved. The momentum of a single particle is \(\vec{p} = m\vec{v}.\) If momentum is conserved, then we expect the total momentum to be constant in a collision. In particular, the momentum before and after a collision between two objects (\(A\) and \(B\)) should be the same: \[\vec{P}_{\tt total} = M_{A} \vec{V}_{A1} + M_{B} \vec{V}_{B1} = M_{A} \vec{V}_{A2} + M_{B} \vec{V}_{B2}\] Momentum is a vector. Conservation of momentum implies that, in two dimensions, the horizontal and vertical components of the total momentum are conserved independently.
Kinetic Energy — The kinetic energy of a particle is \[E = \dfrac{1}{2} MV^2 = \dfrac{P^2}{2M}\] In a perfect elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved. In an inelastic collision, a fraction of kinetic energy is converted to other forms — often heat. We can characterize a collision by looking at the change in energy: \[
E_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} M_A V_{A1}{}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} M_B V_{B1}{}^2
\qquad \qquad \qquad
E_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} M_A V_{A2}{}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} M_B V_{B2}{}^2
\qquad \qquad \qquad
\Delta E = E_2 - E_1
\]

Objectives
Motion lies at the foundation of classical mechanics. In class, we will develop a mathematical description of motion. We will explore this in lab, too. title: Visualizing Motion
text:
Key Ideas
There are four important quantities in kinematics: time, position, velocity, and acceleration. We will denote these by \(t\), \(s(t)\), \(v(t)\), and \(a(t)\) respectively. Position, velocity, and acceleration are related as follows: \[v(t) = \diff{s}{t}
  \qquad \qquad
  a(t) = \diff{v}{t}\] We will not need to take derivatives today. However, this relation allows us to interpret motion graphs as follows:

Velocity is the slope of position; acceleration is the slope of velocity.
If a function is increasing, then its slope is positive (and vice versa).
If a function is decreasing, then its slope is negative (and vice versa).
If a function is constant, then its slope is zero (and vice versa).

Use these ideas today as you try to interpret your motion graphs.

text:
Objectives
Simple machines are devices that change the direction or magnitude of an applied force. Renaissance scholars identified six such machines. We will explore three today: the pulley, the ramp, and the lever.1 Unlike early Renaissance scholars, we have classical mechanics to aid us! We will analyze these devices using forces, work, and energy.

title: Simple Machines
text:
Mechanical Advantage
A simple machine is a device for redirecting or multiplying a force. We often think of such machines in terms of the applied force and the load. The applied force is the force you put into the machine. The load is the force the machine applies to something else. In this lab, it will be the weight you lift.
The mechanical advantage of a machine is the ratio of the load to the applied force:
                           load
mechanical advantage = -------------
                       applied force
For example, if you apply a force of \(100\,\mathsf{lbs}\) and you are able to lift a load of \(200\,\mathsf{lbs}\), the system has a mechanical advantage of 2: It doubles your applied force. In principle, the mechanical advantage is a constant for a particular machine. Thus, if we measure and plot the load as a function of applied force, the mechanical advantage will be the slope of this line.
Note, however, that conservation of energy implies that the work done by each force be equal in magnitude. When a system is in equilibrium, the net work for any small displacement of the system must be zero. This is known as the principle of virtual work.
There are at least three ways to measure forces in this lab. One approach is to use the weight of a known mass. If you hang a \(100\,\mathsf{g}\) mass from a pulley, the applied force will be equal to the weight: \(0.980\,\mathsf{N}\). A second approach is to use a spring scale. A third option is a strain gauge force sensor that connects to the LabQuest interface. You can record and read out force data on LoggerPro.
You may use any of these methods. Be sure to investigate the equipment before you start collecting data. You should understand the proper use and limitations of any equipment you use.

Lever
A lever uses a beam and a fulcrum (a pivot point) to multiply an applied force. It may also redirect the applied force. A Class 1 lever places the load and applied force on opposite sides of the fulcrum — like a teeter-totter or a balance. A Class 2 lever places the load and applied force are on the same side of the fulcrum, with the load closer to the fulcrum — like a crowbar. A Class 3 lever places the load and applied force are on the same side of the fulcrum, with the applied force closer to the fulcrum — like a bicep or a fishing pole.

title: Friction
text:
Static and Kinetic Friction
Despite the complex interactions that give rise to friction, the force obeys a simple law: \[f = \mu N.\] The force due to friction is directly proportional to the normal force acting on an object. The constant of proportionality, \(\mu\), is called the coefficient of friction. If an object is stationary, the constant is called the coefficient of static friction, and the formula gives the maximum force that can be applied before the object starts slipping. If the object is sliding along, it is called the coefficient of kinetic friction. Typically, the coefficient of kinetic friction is less than the coefficient of static friction: it is harder to get something moving than it is to keep it going.
Use a spring scale or a force sensor to investigate this relationship for a wooden block.
Predict. Before you begin, consider the following questions.

What will happen to the force required to move the block if you add mass to it?
What will happen to coefficients of friction if you add mass to the block?
Will the coefficients change if you turn the block on its side?

Measure.

Determine the coefficients of static friction and kinetic friction for the block.
Investigate the dependence on mass and orientation of the block.

Analyze. Summarize your results and discuss your findings in your lab memo.

title: Friction
text:
Critical Angle
Direct measurements with a spring scale or force sensor provide one way to measure the coefficient of friction. A simple alternative is the following.

Place an object on a board.
Tilt the board until the object starts to slide down.
Use Newton’s Second Law and trig to calculate the coefficient of friction.

The maximum angle \(\theta\) to which you can tilt the ramp before the object starts sliding down is called the critical angle. The maximum value for the coefficient of static friction is given by \[\mu = \tan \theta.\]
Test this relationship with the ramps and blocks at your table.
Predict. Discuss the following questions before you begin.

Which will have a larger critical angle on a wooden ramp: wood, rubber, or steel?
Is there a maximum theoretical value for the critical angle?

Analyze. Summarize your results and discuss your findings in your lab memo.

title: Visualizing Motion with Simulations
text:
Key Ideas
There are four important quantities in kinematics: time, position, velocity, and acceleration. We will denote these by \(t\), \(s(t)\), \(v(t)\), and \(a(t)\) respectively. Position, velocity, and acceleration are related as follows: \[v(t) = \diff{s}{t}
  \qquad \qquad
  a(t) = \diff{v}{t}\] We will not need to take derivatives today. However, this relation allows us to interpret motion graphs as follows:

Velocity is the slope of position; acceleration is the slope of velocity.
If a function is increasing, then its slope is positive (and vice versa).
If a function is decreasing, then its slope is negative (and vice versa).
If a function is constant, then its slope is zero (and vice versa).

Use these ideas today as you try to interpret your motion graphs.

Objectives
The mathematical and physical description of rotating objects is fascinating and full of surprises. In this lab, you will carry out a variety of experiments to investigate many of the phenomena associated with rotation. There are three experiments:

title: Rotation and Angular Momentum
text:
Key Ideas
This section briefly describes the fundamental quantities in rotating systems.
Angular Momentum: For a single particle, angular momentum is defined as \[\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}\] Angular momentum is a vector that depends on both the position and momentum of a particle. It points in a direction perpendicular to both. To find the direction of the angular momentum vector, curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation. Your thumb will point in the direction of the angular momentum vector.
Conservation of Angular Momentum: Like energy and momentum, angular momentum is a quantity that is conserved in all interactions. This concept is the key to understanding many of the phenomena in today’s lab.
Moment of Inertia: For a collection of particles like a wheel or pulley, we describe the collective rotational motion with two quantities: the moment of inertia \(I\) and the angular velocity \(\vec{\omega}\). \[\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}\] The angular velocity describes both the direction and speed of rotation. The moment of inertia depends on how the mass of an object is distributed about the rotation axis. The moment of inertia of a single particle rotating around an axis distance \(R\) away is \[I = mR^2.\] The total moment of inertia of an object is the sum of contributions from all of the particles that comprise it.
Torque: Just as a force is required to change the momentum of an object, a torque is required to change the angular momentum of an object. Torque is defined as a moment of force: \[\vec{\tau} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{L}}{\Delta t}
\qquad \qquad
\qquad \qquad
\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}\]
You are not expected to be an expert on these topics, but try to use these concepts in describing the phenomena you observe in today’s lab.

\]
\[
v_n = \dfrac{s_{n+1} - s_{n-1}}{2\Delta t}
\qquad \implies \qquad v(t) \approx \dfrac{s(t+\epsilon) - s(t-\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}
\]
For each approximation, use a Taylor series to approximate \(v(t \pm \epsilon)\) out to terms of order \(\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^3)\). Then, evaluate the fractions. The error of the approximation is the power of the first power of \(\epsilon\) in the resulting expression. For example, saying “the error is linear” means that the coefficient of \(\epsilon\) in the result is not zero; “the error is quadratic” means the coefficient of \(\epsilon\) is zero, but the coefficient of \(\epsilon^2\) is not; and so on. A higher-order error implies a more accurate approximation when \(\epsilon\) is small.
Helmert’s Equation: The acceleration due to gravity is not a universal constant. Read the handout on Helmert's Equation. Use Helmert’s equation to calculate the expected acceleration due to gravity in Klamath Falls, Oregon. Are your data precise enough to measure the deviation from the textbook value? text:
Collisions
In an elastic collision, two objects collide and rebound. In an inelastic collision, they collide and stick together.
Conservation of Momentum — In any collision, Newton’s Second and Third Laws imply that total momentum should be conserved. The momentum of a single particle is \(\vec{p} = m\vec{v}\). If momentum is conserved, then we expect the total momentum to be constant in a collision. In particular, the momentum before and after a collision between two gliders (\(A\) and \(B\)) should be the same: \[\vec{P}_{\tt total} = M_{A} \vec{V}_{A1} + M_{B} \vec{V}_{B1} = M_{A} \vec{V}_{A2} + M_{B} \vec{V}_{B2}\] Note that momentum is a vector, so direction is important.
Kinetic Energy — The kinetic energy of a particle is \(E = \frac{1}{2} mv^2\). In a perfect elastic collision, the total kinetic energy is conserved. In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is converted to other forms — most often, heat.
In this final portion of the lab, the goal is to experimentally determine the degree to which momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. You should collect data for two elastic collisions and two inelastic collisions. title: Measurement and Uncertainty
text:
Random Processes
Many measurements involve randomness and uncertainty. This is often called experimental error, even though they do not imply any mistake in the measurements. Some processes are inherently unpredictable: flipping a coin, rolling a dice, radioactive decay, genetic mutations, earthquakes, the movement of the stock market. But even measuring the length of an aluminum cylinder will not give exactly the same result every time. There may be fluctuations in the length due to vibrations or thermal expansion, and it may be difficult to determine exactly where the end of the bar falls between divisions on your ruler.
Even with randomness and experimental error, we can still summarize a set of observations with two very useful numbers. In this portion of the lab, we will examine a random process and use statistics to summarize our observations.

Qualitative Observations
Open the Plinko Probability simulation from PhET. Select the “Intro” simulation. Press the green Play button to observe the path of a single ball.
You just observed a random walk. The probability of the ball bouncing left or right when it hits a peg is 50 percent. Before you observe more trials, consider the following questions.

Can you predict where the next ball will land?
Are all ending positions equally likely? Or are some positions more likely than others?

Now we are going to make repeated observations of these random walks.

Hit the play button 9 more times, so that you have a total of 10 balls in the bins. Record how many balls are in each bin, and draw or sketch a histogram of this set of observations that shows the number of balls in each bin.
What patterns do you observe?

Now we are going to look at random walks in sets of 10 at a time.

Clear the bins. Select the “\(\times 10\)” option near the Play button. Hit the Play button. Compare the result to your previous histogram of 10 balls. How is it similar? How is it different?
Clear the bins and hit Play at least 4 more times. What patterns do you observe?

Now we are going to look at random walks in sets of 100 at a time.

Clear the bins. Select the “\(\times 100\)” option near the Play button. Hit the Play button. Compare the result to your observations of a single ball and of 10 balls. How is it similar? How is it different?
Clear the bins and hit Play at least 4 more times. What patterns do you observe?

You are starting to see the effect of The Law of Large Numbers. The outcome of any individual random process is unpredictable, but when we make repeated observations of the same process, clear patterns emerge. Now we will use mathematics to explore those patterns.


Statistics
There are two numbers that are useful in describing almost any random process: the mean and the standard deviation. The mean \(\bar{x}\) of a set of numbers is the average value of those numbers. The standard deviation \(s\) quantifies the spread of the data around the mean. Their mathematical definitions are
\[\begin{align*}
\bar{x} & = \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i                        && \text{Mean} \\
s       & = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2} && \text{Standard Deviation}
\end{align*}\]
Open the Plinko Probability simulation from PhET. Select the “Lab” simulation. Play with the simulation to see how it works.

title: Lab Writing Guide
text:
You will be judged in industry not on your work but on how well you communicate your work.
This course gives you practice in a common form of technical writing and in keeping a proper record of your work in a lab notebook. You’ll summarize each week’s activities in a brief memo. The basis of the memo is the information you record in your notebook while carrying out the experiments, simulations, and other group activities.
What follows are guidelines for lab notebooks and memos.

title: Lab Writing Guide
text:
The Lab Notebook
A lab notebook is a permanent record of what you did, when you did it, and how you did it. Lab notebooks are frequently used by researchers to replicate each other’s work and as evidence when assigning priority for discoveries and inventions, so it’s important to keep a proper record of your work. Being able to keep a lab notebook following common conventions in science and industry is a useful skill.
In a professional lab, data and calculations for all experiments must be recorded in a dedicated notebook. The notebook often contains bound sheets of graph paper and remains in the laboratory between sessions. Scientists and engineers use the following conventions in keeping their notebooks:

Write in pen. If you make a mistake, cross it out neatly. Do not erase. Do not tear out sheets.
Reserve the first 2 pages for a Table of Contents. Update it every day.
Write the title of the experiment and the date at the top of each page.
Record your group members’ names for each experiment.
Always record raw data — the numbers you read from an instrument. Always.
Organize data in tables: one quantity per column, one set of measurements and calculations per row.
Include a list of the equipment you used, along with any identifying information.
Include sketches of equipment, circuit diagrams, and block diagrams of your experimental setup.
Calculate results in your notebook. Include a sample calculation.
Include graphs in your notebook. Make them neat, precise, and accurate. Label your axes.
Assign an error or uncertainty to your results. Use an appropriate number of significant figures.
Briefly describe your procedure and make notes to yourself so that you will have a good record later.

Don’t get lost in the details. Focus on the Big Picture: anyone who reads your notebook should be able to reproduce your work and understand your conclusions.

title: Lab Writing Guide
text:
The Memo
Instead of writing a detailed lab report each week, you’ll write a short memorandum, or memo. This is a common form of communication in business, science, and industry.

Memos are written by all “knowledge workers.” They are most often designed to be used within the writer’s own company or organization. They may note the existence of a problem, propose some course of action, describe a procedure, or report the results of a test or an investigation. They are sometimes referred to as informal writing, which is not the same as sloppy, casual, or careless writing. A memo must be carefully prepared, thoughtfully written, and thoroughly proofread for errors.
— from A Survey of Industrial Mathematics by Charles R. MacCluer. Dover (2010). Pages 282–283.

A lab memo is a clear and concise report on your thoughts, work, observations, and conclusions. Communication is the goal. It should be an organized and coherent narrative of what you did and what you learned — after you’ve had a chance to reflect and make sense of it.
You’ll write one lab memo each week. When you finish gathering data and crunching the numbers, outline a short memo. Your memo should be typed, and it’s due 48 hours after your lab session ends. Add it to your portfolio. You may include tables, graphs, and other notes in the Discussion.
Memos follow a standard format. The one we’ll use for this lab is simple.
To:                 [Your Lab Instructor]
                     Department of Natural Sciences
                     Oregon Institute of Technology

From:                [Your Name], Research Assistant
                     [Your Lab Section]

Subject:             [The topic of the memo]

Date:                [Today's Date]

Foreword:


Summary:


Discussion:

The body of your memo should contain three sections:
Foreword: In one or two sentences, describe the problem under investigation. What was the goal of this week’s experiments? Provide a clear and concise overview. Focus on the Big Picture. Save the details for the summary.
Summary: In one or two paragraphs, briefly describe your hypotheses, summarize your procedure, and report your observations. Include numerical results — with appropriate units and significant figures — when relevant.
Discussion: Provide information that an interested reader might need to better understand your summary. A good discussion is at least one paragraph long and does at least one of the following:

Summarize and interpret graphs, drawings, or calculations.
Reflect on the lab. What did you find interesting? Tedious? Frustrating?
Describe technical challenges. What problems did you run into?
Assess your work. How confident are you in your numerical results? How did you quantify uncertainty?
Look ahead. If we were to study this topic further, what would be the next steps?
Describe special equipment you used for the first time.
Improve the lab. Is there a better way to do the experiments or the analyses?

Further Exploration
The following activities are not required. If you have the time and the inclination, you may carry out these investigations for extra credit. You are also free to use any of the materials available in the lab to carry out your own investigations. You need to keep a record of your work (setup, procedure, data, analysis) to get credit for your efforts.
Additional Measurements: Make yet another measurement of the acceleration due to gravity. Some possibilities include the following:

Measure the period of a pendulum. The period of a pendulum is the time it takes the pendulum to swing back and forth once. For small amplitude swings, it is given by \(T = 2\pi
\sqrt{L/g}\). By accurately measuring the length and period of a pendulum, you can deduce the value of \(g\). Note: The “length” of a pendulum, \(L\), is the distance from the pivot point to the center of mass of the swinging object — not necessarily the length of the string you use.
Measure the velocity of cart rolling down a ramp. You can use the LoggerPro software and motion detector, a stopwatch, Tracker, or a method of your own design. For a cart on an incline, Newton’s Second Law predicts that the acceleration down the ramp will be \(a = g \, \sin \theta\).
Use Tracker to measure the acceleration of two different falling objects. Textbook equations imply they should be the same. Are they, to within the uncertainty of the experiment? (Explain what these uncertainties are.) If not, is the problem with the experiment or with the textbook? (Justify your choice.)

Numerical Analysis: An important part of this lab is determining the acceleration from a discrete set of data points. Use calculus to determine the error in the following approximations for the velocity, as a function of the time step \(\epsilon = \Delta t\):
\[
v_n = \dfrac{s_n - s_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
\qquad \implies \qquad v(t) \approx \dfrac{s(t) - s(t-\epsilon)}{\epsilon}
\]
\[
v_n = \dfrac{s_{n+1} - s_{n-1}}{2\Delta t}
\qquad \implies \qquad v(t) \approx \dfrac{s(t+\epsilon) - s(t-\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}
\]
For each approximation, use a Taylor series to approximate \(s(t \pm \epsilon)\) out to terms of order \(\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^3)\). Then, evaluate the fractions. The error of the approximation is the power of the first power of \(\epsilon\) in the resulting expression. For example, saying “the error is linear” means that the coefficient of \(\epsilon\) in the result is not zero; “the error is quadratic” means the coefficient of \(\epsilon\) is zero, but the coefficient of \(\epsilon^2\) is not; and so on. A higher-order error implies a more accurate approximation when \(\epsilon\) is small.
Helmert’s Equation: The acceleration due to gravity is not a universal constant. Read the handout on Helmert's Equation. Use Helmert’s equation to calculate the expected acceleration due to gravity in Klamath Falls, Oregon. Are your data precise enough to measure the deviation from the textbook value? Can Helmert’s equation explain any discrepancy between your data and the standard value?

Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, you should be able to:

Think like a physicist. Apply the fundamental principles of classical mechanics to explain, analyze, and predict real-world phenomena.
Do experiments like a scientist. Keep a record, make careful observations, collect and analyze data, design experiments to test hypotheses, and communicate your findings clearly.
Solve problems. Apply Polya’s problem-solving heuristic. Think critically. Communicate solutions clearly.

title: PHY 221 — Classical Mechanics

Format
This is a studio course: lecture and lab are combined in one class. Physics education research is consistent on one point — you learn physics by doing it, not by watching someone talk about it — so most of our time together is discussion, problem solving, and hands-on lab work. Come prepared: read the assigned material before class, and bring pencil, a calculator, and your laptop or tablet.
A typical class:

Your questions (~10 min)
Quick problems, discussion of key ideas (~20 min)
Group work on problem solving (~30 min)
Lab activity (~60 min)

title: PHY 221 — Classical Mechanics
text:
Grading
Grades shouldn’t get in the way of learning, so this course doesn’t run on point totals. There are three tiers: Fail, Pass (with an argued grade of D, C, or B), and Mastery (A).
To pass, you need all of:

6 labs and lab memos completed satisfactorily
Problem-solving evidence from 6 chapters in each unit
60% or higher on both unit quizzes (Canvas, open book/note, retake as often as you want — only your best score counts)

If you pass, you argue your own grade — D, C, or B — from the evidence in your portfolio: effort, progress, and mastery over the term. Rough guide: D is minimal effort and progress; C is good, regular effort with most work complete; B is strong, consistent effort with a complete, well-organized portfolio.
For an A, you additionally need to pass an A-level exam — a chalk talk or written exam, entirely optional, scheduled during office hours — for each unit. These test whether you can think like a physicist on your own, not whether you can do algebra, query Google, or prompt AI. You can attempt them more than once.
